title: Customers without a usable email
prompt: Return the customers the marketing team cannot email: email is NULL, empty or only spaces. Output customer_id, name.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: customers(customer_id INTEGER, name VARCHAR, email VARCHAR)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: customer_id, name. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: email = NULL is never true: a comparison with NULL is NULL, and WHERE keeps only true rows. Use IS NULL, or fold NULL into a value first with NVL/COALESCE.

starter_source:
-- Bug: customers whose email is NULL are missing.
SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers
WHERE email = NULL OR TRIM(email) = ''

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: What does email = NULL evaluate to?
NVL(TRIM(email), '') turns NULL and blank emails into ''.
explanation: SQL uses three-valued logic: email = NULL is NULL, so WHERE drops the row. IS NULL tests for NULL; NVL(TRIM(email), '') = '' covers NULL, empty and space-only emails in one predicate.
follow_ups: How would you also reject emails without an @?

title: Repeat customers and their late orders
prompt: For each customer with at least 2 orders (any status), return the number of orders and how many of them are LATE. Output customer_id, orders, late_orders.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: orders(order_id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, order_date DATE, status VARCHAR, amount DOUBLE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: customer_id, orders, late_orders. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: A WHERE clause filters rows before GROUP BY, so WHERE status = 'LATE' also changes the order count. Count conditionally with COUNT_IF instead, and filter groups with HAVING.

starter_source:
-- Bug: only LATE orders are counted, so customers with on-time orders drop out.
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(*) AS late_orders
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'LATE'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: Which rows does WHERE remove before the groups are built?
COUNT_IF(condition) counts rows where it is true.
explanation: WHERE runs before GROUP BY and HAVING after it. Counting a subset belongs in the aggregate (COUNT_IF, or SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) so the group keeps all its rows.
follow_ups: Return the late share as a percentage; what does Spark return for 1 / 3?

title: Customers who never ordered: LEFT ANTI JOIN
prompt: Return the customers who have no order at all. Output customer_id, name.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body:
customers(customer_id INTEGER, name VARCHAR, email VARCHAR)
orders(order_id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, order_date DATE, status VARCHAR, amount DOUBLE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: customer_id, name. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: NOT IN (subquery) returns no row at all as soon as the subquery holds a NULL (guest orders have no customer_id). Spark's LEFT ANTI JOIN, like NOT EXISTS, only keeps rows without a match and ignores NULLs.

starter_source:
-- Bug: returns nothing once an order has a NULL customer_id.
SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: Spark has LEFT ANTI JOIN: rows of the left side with no match on the right.
explanation: x NOT IN (3, NULL) is NULL, never true, so one NULL in the subquery empties the result. An anti join (LEFT ANTI JOIN or NOT EXISTS) compares with =, where a NULL key simply never matches.
follow_ups: Rewrite the answer with NOT EXISTS; which plan does Spark choose for each?

title: Latest order per customer with QUALIFY
prompt: Return each customer's latest order, the whole row: the most recent order_date, and the highest order_id when two orders share that date. Output order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: orders(order_id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, order_date DATE, status VARCHAR, amount DOUBLE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: MAX() per column mixes values from different rows (the latest date with another order's amount). Rank the rows in a window and keep the first one; QUALIFY filters on the window without a subquery. RANK keeps every tied row, ROW_NUMBER exactly one.

starter_source:
-- Bug: each column's MAX may come from a different order.
SELECT MAX(order_id) AS order_id, customer_id, MAX(order_date) AS order_date,
       MAX(status) AS status, MAX(amount) AS amount
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: Do MAX(order_date) and MAX(amount) come from the same row?
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) = 1 in a QUALIFY clause.
explanation: Aggregates work column by column, so they cannot pick a row. A window numbers the rows inside each customer; QUALIFY keeps number 1. The tie-breaker (order_id DESC) makes the answer deterministic.
follow_ups: Without QUALIFY (Apache Spark before 4.x), how do you write this with a subquery?

title: Change since the previous reading with LAG
prompt: Meters report readings. For each reading return change: this value minus the same meter's previous value (by reading_date); the first reading of a meter has a NULL change. Output meter_id, reading_date, value, change.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: readings(meter_id VARCHAR, reading_date DATE, value DOUBLE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: meter_id, reading_date, value, change. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: Without PARTITION BY, LAG reads the previous row of the whole table, so a meter's first reading is compared with another meter. Replacing the first NULL with 0 invents a change equal to the whole value.

starter_source:
-- Bug: the previous row may belong to another meter.
SELECT meter_id, reading_date, value,
       value - LAG(value) OVER (ORDER BY meter_id, reading_date) AS change
FROM readings

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: Which rows does LAG see without PARTITION BY?
A meter's first reading has no previous value: keep NULL.
explanation: PARTITION BY restarts the window for every meter, so LAG never crosses from one meter to the next. LAG returns NULL for the first row of a partition, and the prompt keeps that NULL.
follow_ups: Return only the readings whose change is negative (a meter reset).

title: Days to ship: DATEDIFF(end, start)
prompt: For each shipment return days_to_ship, the number of days from order_date to shipped_date (0 when shipped the same day, NULL when not shipped yet). Output order_id, days_to_ship.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: shipments(order_id INTEGER, order_date DATE, shipped_date DATE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: order_id, days_to_ship. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: Spark's DATEDIFF(endDate, startDate) puts the end first, the opposite of T-SQL's DATEDIFF(day, start, end). Swapped arguments give negative durations.

starter_source:
-- Bug: every duration comes out negative.
SELECT order_id, DATEDIFF(order_date, shipped_date) AS days_to_ship
FROM shipments

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: Which argument comes first in Spark's DATEDIFF?
explanation: DATEDIFF(end, start) counts days from start to end. A NULL shipped_date gives NULL, which is what the prompt asks for unshipped orders.
follow_ups: Count the orders shipped within 2 days per week of order_date.

title: Monthly revenue across years: TRUNC to the month
prompt: Return the revenue of each calendar month, as the first day of the month (a DATE) and the sum of amount. Output month, revenue.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: orders(order_id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, order_date DATE, status VARCHAR, amount DOUBLE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: month, revenue. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: MONTH(order_date) is only the month number, so January 2025 and January 2026 land in the same group. TRUNC(order_date, 'MM') keeps the year and returns a DATE; DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', ...) returns a TIMESTAMP.

starter_source:
-- Bug: January 2025 and January 2026 are added together.
SELECT MONTH(order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY MONTH(order_date)

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

explanation: A month bucket needs the year too. TRUNC(order_date, 'MM') maps every date to the first day of its month as a DATE, which groups, sorts and joins to a calendar table cleanly.
follow_ups: Add the months with no order (revenue 0) from a calendar table.

title: Top 2 products per category, ties included
prompt: Return, per category, the products whose revenue is among the 2 highest distinct revenue values of that category (all tied products are kept). Output category, product, revenue.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: sales(category VARCHAR, product VARCHAR, revenue DOUBLE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: category, product, revenue. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: ROW_NUMBER cuts a tie arbitrarily; RANK skips a number after a tie (1, 1, 3) so the second value disappears. DENSE_RANK numbers distinct values (1, 1, 2).

starter_source:
-- Bug: a tie is cut, and which product survives is arbitrary.
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category, product, revenue,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC, product) AS rk
  FROM sales
)
SELECT category, product, revenue FROM ranked WHERE rk <= 2

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: Compare ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK on 50, 50, 20.
The prompt counts distinct revenue values.
explanation: DENSE_RANK gives equal values the same number without gaps, so rk <= 2 keeps every product whose revenue is one of the two highest distinct values.
follow_ups: What changes if the business wants at most 2 products, ties broken by product name?

title: Customers per email domain
prompt: Count the customers per email domain (the part after @), case-insensitively and in lower case. Ignore customers without an email. Output domain, customers.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: customers(customer_id INTEGER, name VARCHAR, email VARCHAR)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: domain, customers. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: String comparison and GROUP BY are case-sensitive in Spark: 'Mail.io' and 'mail.io' are two groups. Normalize with LOWER before grouping; SPLIT_PART(email, '@', 2) is the part after the @.

starter_source:
-- Bug: the same domain in different cases is counted twice.
SELECT SPLIT_PART(email, '@', 2) AS domain, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY SPLIT_PART(email, '@', 2)

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

explanation: GROUP BY compares strings exactly. Lower-casing the domain first puts every spelling of a domain in one group; the WHERE clause drops customers without an email before counting.
follow_ups: Which customers have an email with no @ at all?
